BogSignal / Argos · 15 November 2026

Wetland segmentation:
sensor and temporal experiments

Final report for the completed seed-17 experiments

Executive findings

NISAR added useful weak-reference signal in the controlled sensor comparison. Adding it to Sentinel-2 + Sentinel-1 increased combined swamp/marsh recall by 7.07 percentage points and IoU by 7.81 points. All-sensor model D had the strongest overlap scores among the original four models; model C had the highest recall.

Temporal averaging did not provide a consistent improvement across configurations. It improved recall for Sentinel-2 + NISAR, but the all-sensor averaged-NISAR follow-up missed more reference wetland pixels than D.

Recommendation: retain D as the balanced all-sensor baseline and C as the original recall-oriented alternative. Do not replace D with TD for a recall-focused use case on this evidence. Conclude the current experiment phase; further seeds and independent review belong to follow-up work.

These are validation results against historical/inferred weak labels, not independent contemporary wetland accuracy. Every model uses one training seed. The test set remains unscored.

1. Study question and fixed design

The objective was to classify each pixel in a patch and assess the contribution of Sentinel-1 and NISAR beyond Sentinel-2, followed by a temporal NISAR pilot. The model predicts six classes: Other, Swamp, Marsh, Permanent water, Peatland cropland and Peatland non-cropland. Peatland classes and permanent water are kept separate from the combined swamp/marsh target.

ItemSpecification
Base datasetV4: 3,753 patches; 2,609 train / 585 validation / 559 locked test
Patch grid256 × 256 pixels; 20 m; EPSG:3035; geographic folds and buffers
Optical channelsSentinel-2 B2, B3, B4, B8, B11, B12
Radar channelsS1 ascending/descending VV, VH; NISAR ascending/descending HH, HV
ModelU-Net, ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-34 encoder; six logits; approximately 24.5M parameters
InputsSelected physical channels plus matching validity masks; D and TD: 14 physical + 14 validity = 28 model channels
OptimizationSeed 17; batch 16; AdamW; encoder LR 10⁻⁴, decoder LR 10⁻³; weight decay 10⁻⁴; cosine decay; BF16
Training and selectionCross-entropy, ignore 255; 75/25 minority/background weighted sampling; flips/quarter turns; maximum 50 epochs, minimum 15, patience 10; best validation six-class macro IoU

Normalization is fitted on training data only. Missing normalized predictors are zero-filled, with explicit validity channels. Validation is uniform and unaugmented. Sensor experiments A–D share identical patch IDs, labels and evaluation masks; their configurations differ only by sensor selection, name and output location.

How to read the metrics

For combined wetland inference, sum the Swamp and Marsh probabilities first, then choose among Other, combined Wetland, Permanent water, Peatland cropland and Peatland non-cropland. This is an inference-only merge of a six-class model; no five-class retraining was performed. Every eligible pixel receives a class. There is no ranking, area budget or tuned threshold in the main tables.

  • Recall: fraction of reference swamp/marsh pixels recovered. A Swamp–Marsh subtype swap is accepted in the combined target.
  • Reference precision: fraction of predicted swamp/marsh pixels overlapping the weak positive labels. Missing wetland labels can depress this value.
  • F2: combines precision and recall, weighting recall more heavily. Higher recall alone is insufficient.
  • F1 and IoU: measure combined-class agreement/overlap. Six-class macro IoU separately averages the original six classes.

Primary NISAR contrast, D − B: recall +7.07 points, reference precision +14.11, F2 +8.24 and wetland IoU +7.81; six-class macro IoU +1.10. These results support a useful NISAR contribution in this run, without establishing statistical significance.

Objective matters: C reaches 45.09% recall, while D reaches 39.62% recall with much higher reference precision (48.23% versus 33.90%) and higher IoU (27.80% versus 24.00%). D is the balanced baseline; C remains the original recall-oriented alternative. Adding S1 to C did not improve recall.

3. Temporal NISAR pilot

The pilot acquired 120 provisional GCOV products across 24 coverage groups: one selected observation per month from June through October. The selected window is 18 June–20 October 2026. Ascending/descending passes and anchor tracks/frames remain separate. At least three jointly valid HH/HV observations are required per pixel and pass; valid pixels use three, four or five dates.

T0 uses the latest valid date; T1 averages linear radar power before conversion to dB; T2 adds clipped-dB population standard deviation and p10/p90 from the same dates. S2 and S1 stay static. T0/T1/T2 select S2 + NISAR channels; TB is a matched static S2 + S1 reference. TB is not a pure test of incremental NISAR because the sensor combinations differ.

Matched dataset: 2,578 train / 543 validation / 525 locked test; 107 original candidate patches were excluded by declared validity rules. All four rows below share identical validation IDs, labels and masks: 34,690,287 scored pixels. Do not directly subtract these rows from the original A–D table: the eligible footprint and processing regime changed.

T1 · S2 + mean NISAR35.54%46.87%42.53%44.60%45.93%28.70%

Averaging, T1 − T0: recall +6.11 points, precision −1.72, F2 +4.52 and IoU +1.76. T1 is the best recall-oriented representation within this matched temporal pilot. Adding variability features raised precision but reduced recall and F2. Coarse percentiles from three to five dates do not establish annual hydrological extremes.

4. All-sensor follow-up: averaged NISAR versus D

TD uses static Sentinel-2 + static Sentinel-1 + averaged NISAR. It trained for 41 epochs, selecting epoch 31. The existing D checkpoint was reused and rescored on the same 543 validation patches and 34,690,287 valid pixels as TD. Patch IDs, common labels and baseline validity were checked; no D retraining or checkpoint reselection was performed.

ModelSix-class macro IoUWetland recallReference precisionF1F2Wetland IoU
D · original NISAR, common area35.48%39.75%49.40%44.05%41.36%28.25%
TD · averaged NISAR, common area35.50%35.00%56.06%43.10%37.85%27.47%

TD − D: recall −4.75 points, precision +6.66, F2 −3.52 and wetland IoU −0.78. Six-class macro IoU was effectively unchanged (+0.02 points). TD is more conservative: it has higher reference precision but misses more labelled wetland pixels. This run does not support replacing D for recall-focused use.

This is a practical comparison against the existing baseline, not an isolated test of averaging. D trained on 2,609 patches with validated NISAR P05036 / 1.0.20 / 1.6.0; TD trained on 2,578 patches with provisional P05023 / 1.0.11 / 1.5.0. Dates, processing maturity, training normalization and sampling populations differ. A same-footprint, same-processing all-sensor latest-date run would be needed to isolate averaging.

D’s numbers here differ slightly from section 2 because it is rescored on a smaller shared validation area, not because D was changed.

5. Candidate ranking for targeted review

Ranking answers a different question: if we can inspect only a small fraction of the scored area, where should we look first? Use each pixel’s score pSwamp + pMarsh, order pixels from highest to lowest, and take the highest-scoring pixels within a fixed area budget. This produces a review-priority layer; it does not change the ordinary five-class inference map.

How to read D at a 5% area budget

Inspecting the highest-scoring 5% of the common validation area would recover 73.40% of its reference swamp/marsh pixels—about 73 of every 100 labelled wetland pixels. Of the selected pixels, 24.07% overlap the weak wetland labels, compared with 1.64% prevalence over the whole scored area. The remaining selected pixels are not all verified errors: the reference labels are incomplete.

At 1% of area, D recovers 32.79% of reference wetland pixels; expanding review to 10% recovers 86.33%. More coverage costs more review effort and reduces reference precision.

Ordering pixels well and assigning a wetland class at the fixed argmax decision are different uses of the scores. Compare ranking rows within each panel; the original and temporal panels have different eligible footprints and processing regimes.

Budgets apply only to the fixed scored validation area, not the full AOI. Whole equal-score groups are retained only when they fit, so selected area never exceeds the declared budget. Average precision is exact, non-interpolated, and computed over distinct score thresholds. The 1%, 5%, 10% and 20% budgets were fixed for evaluation; no threshold was optimized for these tables. Scores are not established calibrated wetland probabilities. These pixel selections do not establish object-level site detection, independent discovery accuracy or restoration suitability.

TD’s completed analysis evaluated ordinary classification only; it has no saved candidate-ranking evaluation and is deliberately omitted here. No new inference or training was performed to add this section. The test set remains unscored.

7. Interpretation, limitations and stopping point

  • Weak references: labels are historical/inferred and can be incomplete, wrong or temporally mismatched. Other is not verified dry land. Precision and recall both describe agreement with these references.
  • One seed: no repeated-seed uncertainty or spatial confidence intervals were estimated. Millions of correlated pixels do not constitute millions of independent samples. Small differences should remain inconclusive.
  • Validation reuse: checkpoints and subsequent representations were considered using validation performance. Results are exploratory model-development findings, not a final generalization estimate. The locked test has not been scored.
  • Temporal quality: provisional NISAR maturity, residual RFI, irregular timing and only three to five valid dates limit interpretation. Existing spatial exclusions do not certify every provisional date as artifact-free.
  • Task scope: combined swamp/marsh detection is easier than correct subtype classification. These experiments do not establish restoration suitability, object-level site detection or independent discovery accuracy.
  • Numerical checks: frozen-checkpoint inference preserved hashes and scoring support and passed the 0.1-percentage-point engineering tolerance. BF16/cuDNN benchmarking is not bitwise deterministic; that tolerance is not statistical uncertainty.

Final conclusion: the controlled baseline experiments indicate useful additional NISAR information. Simple temporal averaging helped the S2 + NISAR configuration, but the improvement did not carry over to the all-sensor comparison against D. The defensible outcome is a working baseline and a documented precision–recall tradeoff, not a universal temporal-model improvement.

Stop new experiments for this submission. Preserve D, C and the temporal checkpoints and report the observed results and limits. After the deadline, prioritize repeated seeds, independent spatial review and a matched-processing all-sensor temporal control before more complex architectures. No new training or test evaluation was performed to build this report.

8. Reproducibility and retained artifacts

All nine trained checkpoints are retained with frozen configurations, dataset hashes, learning curves and evaluation artifacts. The new comparison checks align patch IDs and reject changed labels or pixels invalid for D. The repository test suite passed 56 tests. Retention is confirmed; this report does not claim that an off-machine backup was created.
